problems.form_value: Pools are not split by writer background, so L1 and L2 metaphors in one condition share a centroid; Fig. 2A then splits the per-metaphor scores by writer group.
problems.source_says: The paper never says whether L1 and L2 metaphors share a centroid. Methods say only 'same scenario in the same condition', and Results speak of each group's own pool. The numbers do not fit a shared centroid. With one, the pooled AI ideation mean must be a weighted average of the S1 group means (L1 0.457, L2 0.451), about 0.454, because L2 writers are roughly half of that arm (p. 8: 84 of 228 L2 writers, 39% in AI ideation, 34% in AI refinement). The simulation section prints 0.457 for that pool (p. 10), and Fig. 3D puts the No AI and refinement pools (about 0.414 and 0.422) about 0.004 above their weighted averages too. Form-spec rule 1 bars the inference. The point matters: it decides whether S1-O1 is the codebook section 8 measure 'across all participants in each arm'. If the pools are split by background, only the figure-only arm-level human pools in Fig. 3A and 3D are.
problems.quote: In contrast, AI ideation compressed both groups’ pools and narrowed the gap between them

confirmed: Every outcome is scored on the writers' submitted metaphors: by sentence embeddings or a type-token ratio (S1-O1 to S1-O5), by 351 blinded Prolific evaluators (S1-O6, S1-O7), or by LLM judges (S1-O8). None is self-reported (p. 16, Evaluators; p. 18, Evaluation task and Collective diversity measure; p. 27, Figs. S9-S10).

S1-O1 and S1-O2 are per-metaphor leave-one-out centroid similarities (metaphor text only is primary, metaphor plus explanation is secondary), analyzed in a mixed model with writer and scenario intercepts on 2,493 observations. So construct diversity, measure embedding_similarity, unit output, and n_units 2493 hold (pp. 18-19, Collective diversity measure and Statistical analysis; Tab. S1, p. 28).

Tab. S3 values match: centroid similarity, AI refinement (vs ideation) -0.037 (-0.052 to -0.023), p < 0.001, N writer 440, 1,707 observations; divergent rating -1.31 (-3.21 to 0.60), p = 0.178, N evaluator 351, N writer 441, 5,638 observations (p. 29, Tab. S3).

S1-O6 and S1-O7 use the rating model (random intercepts for evaluator, writer, and scenario; 8,241 observations), so unit rating and n_units 8241 hold. Novelty plus surprise fits construct novelty, appropriateness plus explanation quality fits usefulness, and lay Prolific evaluators fit human_raters (p. 18, Evaluation task; p. 19, Statistical analysis; Tab. S2, pp. 28-29).

Every Tab. S2 number in S1-O6 and S1-O7 matches, including the intercepts 53.41 and 63.65, as do the text values 4.753 and 0.834, 2.930 and -3.138, 3.127 and 3.711, 3.241 and -1.756, and 1.485, p = 0.219 (p. 28, Tab. S2; p. 12, Results).

The quantile-regression values match p. 13 (7.5 at tau = 0.1 and 4.5 at tau = 0.9; 6.3 at tau = 0.1 and 5.1 at tau = 0.2; L2 convergent 2.6 at tau = 0.9, p = 0.048). The Fig. S4 stars for L1 convergent AI refinement fall at five quantiles between 0.2 and 0.7, as the text says (p. 13; p. 25, Fig. S4).

S1-O8: the Fig. S10A cells read 0.32, 0.37, and 0.30 against the human panel (caption 0.31 to 0.38) and 0.68 to 0.87 among the judges. In Fig. S10B all three LLM judges score AI ideation above No AI and AI refinement below it, while the human panel scores both above No AI (p. 27, Fig. S10, rendered at 450 dpi; caption pp. 27-28).

The Fig. S9 readings for S1-O4 and S1-O5 match the form: semantic distance is lowest under AI ideation for both groups, with bars clear of No AI, and the refinement bars overlap or touch No AI; TTR is flat for L1, and for L2 it is higher under ideation (bars meet) and lower under refinement (bars overlap). In S1-O3, AI ideation is lower than No AI for both groups (p. 27, Fig. S9, rendered at 400 and 700 dpi).

AI availability 'yes' and timing 'immediate' hold for S1. Ideation writers saw five GPT-4o metaphors before composing (p. 17). Refinement writers typed their metaphor into the AI chat, which the L1 prompt bars from suggesting it, then received AI explanations (p. 18; Fig. S7, p. 26). The AI translated the text of L2 writers who used their native language (p. 18). Everything happens in one session of median 20 minutes (p. 16), so no after_ai outcome exists.

Given the recorded constructs, every S1 question follows the codebook rule (diversity is across_people, the rest with_ai), and S2-O1 'none' follows the form-spec field note for AI output compared with human output (codebook section 1; form-spec, Field notes, question).

The S2-O1 numbers match: Claude Δ = 0.102, Qwen Δ = 0.111, GPT-4o mini Δ = 0.241, all p < 0.001; 75.3% of the human-only pool's diversity; M = 0.528 vs. 0.457, Δ = 0.071, p < 0.001; plateau around 0.50 with a gap of 0.04; 14.3% gibberish and format adherence below 75% (pp. 9-10, Results).

Apart from the arm-level human pools noted under S1-O1, no creativity or diversity outcome on participants' output is missing. The paper reports only the two rating subscales, not single items. The L2 language splits are self-selected and sit in notes. The GPT-2 perplexity of the human pools in Fig. 3D is a fluency check that the paper does not treat as creativity or diversity (p. 9, Fig. 3D; p. 10, Fig. 3 caption; p. 18).
summary: Eligibility holds: S1 scores the writers' own metaphors with embedding-based centroid similarity and with blinded evaluator ratings, and every printed coefficient, interval, p-value, mean, and N that the form records matches the PDF. The coding is still refuted on detail, because the units of S1-O3 to S1-O5, the constructs of S1-O4 and S1-O5, and the claim that L1 and L2 metaphors share one centroid rest on inferences the paper does not state, S1-O3's reported text omits a non-overlapping L2 drop under AI refinement, and S2-O1 codes no contrast against the human-only pool.
